title: Cautions
hook: the Kalamas: test a teaching yourself, and trust no one who asks for secrecy or blind obedience (AN 3.65)

segments.voice: Yesterday: kalyanamitta, and your line, the whole of the path. Did you tell your admirable friend one thing they gave you? Day three hundred twenty-one.

You met the Kalamas back in the story camp. Their town, Kesaputta, was one teachers kept passing through. Each one, the sutta says, explained his own teaching and made it shine, and ran down everyone else's. Then the next one came and did the same. The Kalamas were left with a plain, tired question: which of these people is telling the truth? When the Buddha came through, they asked him exactly that. His answer is often quoted, and often quoted wrong. Today: cautions.
screen: `TEACHERS KEEP PASSING THROUGH.` → `EACH ONE RUNS DOWN THE LAST.` → `WHICH OF THEM IS RIGHT?`

segments.voice: First, the Buddha tells the Kalamas that their doubt is reasonable. Then he gives a list, here in paraphrase. Don't go by reports, or by tradition, or by hearsay. Don't go by scripture, or by logic, or by inference, or by what merely seems plausible, or by a view you already like. Don't go by how impressive a speaker is, or by the thought, this is our teacher. Instead, when you know for yourselves that certain things are unwholesome, blamed by the wise, and lead to harm and suffering when you act on them, let them go. When you know that things are wholesome, praised by the wise, and lead to well-being, take them up. Then he asks them questions. Does greed lead to benefit or harm? Hatred? Delusion? And they answer for themselves. Notice what the sutta does not say. It isn't believe whatever feels right. It points to results you can watch in your own life, and to the judgment of wise people. Test it yourself, with your eyes open. There's a second caution, and it comes from other texts, not this one. In a short discourse the Buddha says the sun, the moon and his teaching shine openly; they aren't hidden. And near the end of his life he said he had never held back anything in a closed fist. Some traditions keep certain practices for students who have prepared, as you saw in the Tibetan weeks. That's different from secrecy about money, or about how people are treated, or demands for obedience that override your conscience. Those are warning signs anywhere. Test it yourself.
screen: `YOUR DOUBT IS REASONABLE.` · `KNOW FOR YOURSELVES.` · `WATCH THE RESULTS, ASK THE WISE.` · `THE TEACHING SHINES OPENLY.` · then, large: `TEST IT YOURSELF.`

segments.voice: Before the sit, think of one warning sign you'd want to remember, in any group, spiritual or not. Maybe it's being told not to ask questions. Maybe it's money nobody explains, or being pulled away from friends. Pick one, and after the sit, write it down. Then sit with the breath, and notice something you can test right now: does this breath, watched closely, bring agitation or ease? Just look. The bell holds the time.
Cautions. The Buddha told the Kalamas to know for themselves, by results and by the wise, and his teaching shines openly, not in secret.
Your line: test it yourself. Today, take one thing you've heard on this path and check it against your own day: does it lead to harm, or to ease? Day three hundred twenty-one.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often cite the Kalama Sutta to encourage students to test the teaching in their own experience, and many communities publish codes of conduct and financial information so that students can check a group openly.

match.prompt: match the cautions to where they come from.

myth: the Kalama Sutta says believe whatever feels right to you
it points to results you can watch and to the judgment of the wise.
the Buddha told the Kalamas not to go even by scripture
scripture is on the list, alongside tradition, logic and a teacher's reputation.
the warning about secrecy comes from the Kalama Sutta itself
it echoes other texts: the teaching shining openly, and no closed fist.

fork.setup: you're a Kalama. teacher after teacher says only his way is true. you ask the Buddha whom to believe. what does he tell you?
options: know for yourselves, by results and the judgment of the wise.
fork.reveal: he says their doubt is reasonable, and asks them to see for themselves whether greed, hatred and delusion lead to harm.

original.note: Pali Kālāma: the clan of Kesaputta who asked the Buddha whom to believe (AN 3.65).

trapdoor: what you thought: the Buddha said to trust your gut.
what it means: test a teaching by its results in your life and by the judgment of the wise.
what a scholar hears: the ten grounds not to rely on include piṭaka-sampadāna, 'the authority of a text'; the openness theme is AN 3.129 and the 'teacher's closed fist' (ācariya-muṭṭhi) of DN 16.

sources.ref: Anguttara Nikaya 3.129 (three things that shine openly)
Digha Nikaya 16, Mahaparinibbana Sutta 2.25 (no teacher's closed fist)

notes: Added 2026-10-06 from the five-year map: the hook now points back to day 66 ('The Kalamas ask'), which tells the sutta's four comforts; today keeps the list of what not to rely on. Confirm with the Keeper.

The index hook attributes the secrecy and blind-obedience warning to AN 3.65; the Kalama Sutta itself doesn't contain it. The script says so and draws on AN 3.129 and DN 16 instead. Suggest the index hook be adjusted.
Kalama Sutta list paraphrased; the ten items and their order vary slightly by translation.
The line distinguishing restricted Vajrayana transmissions from harmful secrecy should be checked by a Tibetan Keeper.
DN 16 section number (2.25 in Rhys Davids' numbering) for 'closed fist': confirm.
